questions.q: What question does high availability (HA) answer that disaster recovery (DR) does not?
options: What happens when a single node or rack fails locally, within the same datacenter/region
What happens when an entire Azure region becomes unreachable
How to grant the least amount of access needed to a database
How often full backups should run
questions.explain: HA is about surviving a local failure with minimal or no downtime. DR is about surviving a regional disaster, typically with some planned downtime and data loss.

questions.q: How does the Azure SQL Database General Purpose tier achieve HA?
options: By separating compute from remote, redundant storage — a failed compute node reattaches to the same durable storage
By running a cluster of nodes each with independent local storage kept in sync
By geo-replicating the entire database to a different Azure region
It has no HA mechanism at all
questions.explain: General Purpose's architecture keeps the data on remote storage separate from compute, so HA means swapping the compute node, not the storage.

questions.q: How does the Business Critical tier's HA mechanism differ from General Purpose's?
options: It uses a cluster of multiple nodes, each with its own local storage, continuously kept in sync — any replica can take over almost instantly
It has no compute/storage separation and no replicas at all
It relies entirely on nightly full backups for HA
It is identical to General Purpose's architecture
questions.explain: Business Critical trades the remote-storage model for a standing group of synchronized replicas with fast local storage, enabling near-instant failover.

questions.q: Why is neither the General Purpose nor the Business Critical HA architecture, by itself, disaster recovery?
options: Both architectures operate within a single region — if that whole region goes down, a separate mechanism like geo-replication or failover groups is needed
Because HA and DR are actually the exact same thing described differently
Because Business Critical is only available in one specific Azure region worldwide
Because General Purpose does not support any form of redundancy
questions.explain: Both service-tier architectures solve HA within a region. Surviving a regional disaster requires a separate, DR-specific mechanism covered later in this chapter.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 14 treat HA and DR as separate problems with separate tools rather than one topic?
options: Because each answers a different failure scenario (local vs. regional) and Azure SQL provides genuinely different mechanisms for each — mixing them up leads to a system that only survives one kind of outage
Because Microsoft requires DBAs to memorize two unrelated glossaries for the exam
Because HA is only relevant to on-premises SQL Server and DR only to Azure SQL Database
Because there is no meaningful difference and the split is purely arbitrary
questions.explain: A DBA who treats HA and DR as interchangeable risks building a system that handles a node failure but not a regional disaster, or vice versa.
